docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Inference pods: models · serving engines · user-space libraries
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Kubernetes: kubelet · CRI · Cilium networking and policy
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OuterSpace OS: Ubuntu kernel · systemd · containerd · Dragonfly
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Bare metal / virtual machine

docs.title: Image layout
docs.text:
Partition Purpose Status EFI system partition systemd-boot and unified kernel image Unsigned development boot assets OOS_ROOT Read-only ext4 host filesystem dm-verity data OOS_VERITY Root hash tree Expected hash embedded in UKI OOS_STATE Persistent /var Runtime images, kubelet identity, bounded logs

A trusted root hash is necessary for authenticity. Development UKIs are unsigned; Secure Boot signing is a release gate. The current image has one root slot. Authenticated A/B updates, boot health checks and rollback are planned together. There are no in-place apt upgrades on the running host.

docs.title: Runtime and networking
docs.text:
containerd uses overlayfs, systemd cgroups and the CRI API. Kubelet is configured with anonymous authentication disabled, webhook authorization, TLS bootstrap, certificate rotation and default seccomp. CNI binaries and configuration live in persistent state through fixed paths in the read-only filesystem.

Cilium is the first eBPF integration. Its trusted agents need privileges; host policy disables unprivileged BPF. Kernel BPF/BTF features are checked at build time. A local three-node kind lab validates cross-node DNS/service connectivity and network-policy deny/restore. That lab uses Docker's kernel and does not qualify the OuterSpace OS kernel as a joined cluster node.

docs.title: Image and model delivery
docs.text:
Dragonfly is enabled by node configuration with explicit registry routing. Containerd retains HTTPS origin resolution and digest verification. Each node still stores the image content needed by its containers. P2P reduces repeated traffic from origin; it does not make local storage unnecessary.

Kubelet owns unused image garbage collection (24h maximum age, 80%/65% pressure thresholds). Its age tracking resets on kubelet restart. Dragonfly's peer cache has a separate six-hour TTL. No external prune loop competes with kubelet.

Model weights are a separate lifecycle: an image being ready does not mean weights are loaded into RAM or VRAM. Measure image delivery, model loading and inference readiness independently. End-to-end P2P, private registry authorization and GPU profiles remain qualification work.

The source design records detailed decisions and references.

docs.title: Is this a container image?
docs.text: It is an operating-system disk image, assembled from Ubuntu packages. Containers are the workloads it hosts. The first image targets worker nodes.

docs.title: Can it replace the OS in an AKS node pool?
docs.text: No. Managed AKS requires its supported node images. OuterSpace can be tested on Azure VMs in self-managed Kubernetes, while portable applications can also run on AKS.

docs.title: Does P2P eliminate images on every machine?
docs.text: Each node still needs the layers it executes. Dragonfly can reduce repeated origin traffic by sharing content between peers. Model-weight storage remains separate.

docs.title: When are unused images removed?
docs.text: Kubelet owns runtime GC with a configured 24-hour maximum unused age and 80%/65% disk-pressure thresholds. Age tracking resets when kubelet restarts. Dragonfly's peer cache uses a separate six-hour TTL. These policies still need lifecycle tests.

docs.title: Is GPU inference supported?
docs.text: A GPU profile is planned. Driver/kernel compatibility, signed modules, CDI and a real inference test on hardware must be validated before claiming support.

docs.title: Is it production ready or CIS certified?
docs.text: No. It is a development foundation with explicit qualification gates. There is no stable release or completed CIS audit.

docs.title: Is it a Flatcar fork?
docs.text: No. It takes inspiration from the small, immutable container-host approach and assembles its own image from Ubuntu packages.

docs.title: Capabilities and status
docs.text:
Area Implemented foundation Still to qualify Minimal host Ubuntu package assembly, no desktop or model framework Hardware-specific footprint and firmware Immutable root Read-only ext4 with dm-verity Signed boot, tamper tests, A/B rollback Kubernetes runtime containerd, kubelet, CRI tools OS node enrollment and real inference pod eBPF Kernel checks, Cilium profile, local kind policy test Cilium on an enrolled OuterSpace node Image delivery Native Dragonfly peer, explicit registry routing P2P metrics, outage cases, private auth, peer security Cache cleanup Kubelet max age/pressure and separate peer TTL Long-running GC, restart and disk-pressure tests Hardening Accounts locked, AppArmor, seccomp defaults, audit and sysctls CIS audit, tailoring, enforcement and vulnerability evidence Accelerators CPU foundation GPU kernel/driver/CDI profile and hardware tests Releases Version and evidence gate validator Qualified preview artifacts, signing and supported stable branch

No latency, image-size reduction percentage or CIS compliance score is published without a reproducible measurement. See security and release qualification.

docs.title: Build a development image
docs.text:
Requirements: Python 3.11+, Make and Docker running Linux containers. The build uses the Docker VM's native architecture: arm64 on Apple Silicon, amd64 on CI. Allow several gigabytes for package caches and build output.

git clone https://github.com/Alien6-Studio/outerspace-os.git
cd outerspace-os
make check
make builder
make build
make smoke

The disposable builder uses privileged Linux mount namespaces. It has no host devices or Docker socket mounted. QEMU verification needs no additional privileges.

The build/ directory contains a raw GPT disk, UKI, split kernel/initrd, package manifest and boot log. Development images are unsigned. Do not overwrite a physical disk to try this first version; use the snapshot-based QEMU smoke test.

The smoke test checks read-only root, verity mapping, writable state, cgroup v2, BPF/BTF availability, AppArmor, selected hardening settings, locked operator account and CRI availability. It boots the split kernel/initrd, not the EFI boot path.

docs.title: Configure a worker
docs.text:
The repository includes a config-drive generator. It accepts a real cluster CA, a short-lived bootstrap token read from a protected file, and an HTTPS API address. It validates input and produces private files. No password is baked into the image.

python3 scripts/node-config.py \
  --api-server https://api.example.net:6443 \
  --ca /secure/cluster-ca.crt \
  --token-file /secure/bootstrap-token \
  --cluster-dns 10.96.0.10
./scripts/config-drive.sh

The generated drive contains credentials. Attach it only to the intended node, detach after enrollment and revoke the token. Cluster enrollment on this image is still a release gate. See the repository guide.

docs.title: Operator identity
docs.text: The image includes an outerspace account (UID 1000), locked by default. Root is also locked; no SSH server, shared password, sudo or autologin is installed. An explicit, audited administrative-access design is required before hardware rollout. The ASCII boot banner identifies the distribution and development version.

docs.title: A Linux host with one mission
docs.text:
OuterSpace OS is an Ubuntu-based operating system for Kubernetes inference workers, installed on bare metal or tested in virtual machines. A small host supplies Linux, systemd, containerd and kubelet. Inference engines, model frameworks and user-space accelerator libraries belong in containers.

Development — 0.1.0-dev.0

There is no stable release, supported production image or CIS certification. The source and tests are available; hardware qualification, secure updates and security audit evidence are still required.

The first foundation uses Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, a generic server kernel, a read-only root protected by dm-verity, and a writable /var for runtime state. Native Dragonfly integration provides optional P2P image delivery. Cilium supplies the cluster networking and policy profile.

docs.title: Where it fits
docs.text:
• Physical inference workers in self-managed Kubernetes / kubeadm clusters.
  • Virtual machines for image qualification and self-managed cloud clusters.
  • Local Docker/kind tests for cluster integration, separately from OS image tests.

Managed AKS node pools require provider-supported OS images. OuterSpace cannot replace their base OS. On Azure, test this OS on VMs running a self-managed cluster; AKS can separately test portable workloads and supported cluster components.

Start with the build guide, architecture, and release policy.

docs.title: Releases and maintenance
docs.text:
Current status: 0.1.0-dev.0. No stable or public alpha release exists.

OuterSpace uses its own MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version, independent of the Ubuntu, Linux kernel and Kubernetes versions. It follows familiar prerelease conventions:

0.1.0-dev.0 → 0.1.0-alpha.1 → 0.1.0-beta.1 → 0.1.0-rc.1 → 0.1.0

A tagged build is not automatically a supported release. Each stage requires version- and commit-specific evidence. The validator refuses missing gates and refuses publishing a -dev.N version as a release.

docs.title: Qualification phases
docs.text:
Phase Intended use Required evidence Development Internal engineering and disposable labs Unit/contract checks and image build logs Alpha Explicit experimental preview Boot, CRI, config contract, checksums, release notes and license/source review Beta Integration testing Alpha gates plus Node Ready, Cilium, P2P, GC and state persistence Release candidate Frozen candidate for qualification Beta gates plus bare metal, CIS audit, signed boot, upgrade/rollback, SBOM and vulnerability review Stable Supported operation within a published matrix RC gates plus soak tests and an explicit support policy

Release CI prepares draft releases after verification. Maintainer review and complete evidence are required before publication. Stable status is never inferred from a green build or a tag. No automatic promotion between stages occurs.

docs.title: Maintenance model
docs.text:
• Rebuild images from reviewed Ubuntu security/update packages; deploy whole images.
  • Pin runtime binaries and verify SHA256. Review kernel ABI and dependent modules together.
  • Run regular integration builds to detect package and upstream drift.
  • Review dependency updates in pull requests, including release notes and migration risks.
  • Record exact package manifests, runtime versions, architecture and source commit.
  • Qualify upgrade, downgrade and persistent-state compatibility before promotion.

Prelaunch work has no production support commitment. A stable branch must state its support dates, architectures, kernel/runtime/Kubernetes matrix and security response ownership before it can pass the support gate. Upstream Ubuntu LTS coverage does not automatically confer support on this distribution.

docs.title: Launch sequence
docs.text:
1. Publish source and clearly marked development documentation.
  2. Qualify and publish alpha artifacts with known limitations.
  3. Validate on a dedicated bare-metal worker, then a self-managed cloud VM cluster.
  4. Complete beta integration and RC security/update gates.
  5. Publish support policy and stable artifacts with checksums, SBOM and provenance.
  6. Only then apply to distribution directories with accurate status and licensing.

The authoritative release policy and evidence contract live with the build source. There is no downloadable stable image at this stage.

docs.title: Security target
docs.text:
The target is CIS Ubuntu Linux 24.04 LTS v2.0.0, Level 1 Server, with explicit Kubernetes/eBPF tailoring. CIS is the Center for Internet Security. Its benchmarks provide configuration recommendations; choosing them is not a certification.

The image includes a read-only verity root, locked local accounts, no SSH server, AppArmor availability, Kubernetes seccomp defaults, kernel-introspection restrictions, audit rules and bounded logs. Runtime enforcement still requires testing.

docs.title: Material development limitations
docs.text:
• UKIs are unsigned; dm-verity alone does not establish boot authenticity.
  • The state partition is unencrypted.
  • There is no authenticated A/B updater or rollback implementation yet.
  • Full CIS host and Kubernetes audit evidence is absent.
  • Private P2P registry authorization and peer security remain unqualified.

docs.title: Evidence before claims
docs.text:
Run Canonical USG with a suitable Ubuntu Pro subscription and a reviewed tailoring file on a disposable image instance. Preserve audit output. Select a Kubernetes benchmark that matches the actual Kubernetes version and retain worker results. Translate accepted remediations into the image build; do not blindly mutate an enrolled worker with an audit tool's fix command.

Document every exception with applicability, rationale, owner, review date and supporting tests. IP forwarding, trusted BPF agents and executable container state need workload-aware policies. Never omit a rule solely to improve a score.

For the full target, see security documentation. For sensitive reports, use GitHub's private reporting feature if enabled; otherwise request a private reporting channel without posting exploit details publicly.

docs.title: OuterSpace OS by Alien6
docs.text:
OuterSpace OS is a distribution project by Alien6, focused on a small, purpose-built host for Kubernetes inference workers.

The visual identity retains its original planetary illustration and pink/violet palette. The faceted orbital mark and ASCII boot banner connect the website with the operating system. The footer follows the same “by Alien6” attribution used by Trunx, Signal and Ruleflow.

Development happens in the GitHub repository. The distribution source lives on main; website source and generated pages live on gh-pages. Original OuterSpace source is licensed under Apache-2.0. Ubuntu packages and bundled upstream components retain their own licenses.
